:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
If
${A} = 
    \left\lbrack
    \begin{matrix}
        2 & -1  \\
        -3 & k
    \end{matrix}
    \right\rbrack$
and
$\det({A}) = 5$, what is the value of $k?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
For a $2 \times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix} = ad - bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -3 & k\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot k-(-1)\cdot (-3) \\  & =2k-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(A)=5,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =5 \\ 2k-3 & =5 \\ 2k & =8 \\ k & =4\end{aligned}
$$

and $det(D)=-32$, what is the value of $x?$

For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
|\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}|=ad-bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D) & =|\begin{aligned}2x & 6 \\ 2x & x-2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2x\cdot (x-2)-6\cdot 2x \\  & =2{x}^{2}-16x\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(D)=-32$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D) & =-32 \\ 2{x}^{2}-16x & =-32 \\ 2{x}^{2}-16x+32 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-8x+16 & =0 \\ (x-4)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The **determinant** of a general $2 \times 2$ matrix
$\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix}$
is denoted $\text {det} ({A})$ and computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}
$$

For example, given the matrix
$\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ 
the determinant is

$$
\det(A) = {\color{blue}{2}} \cdot {\color{blue}{3}} - {\color{red}{1}} \cdot {\color{red}{5}} = 1.
$$

To remember how to compute the determinant of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, you can imagine taking the product of the diagonal of the matrix, and then subtracting the product of the off-diagonal terms, as follows:

![](images/25/2594f99e0f02241dc6d01f85c82923103df1d6fb4dda5ca03d438637f5178a28.png)

Later, we will see that the determinant is related to the "volume" spanned by the row vectors or column vectors in a matrix. We will also see that the determinant can tell us about many other properties of a matrix. 

However, in this lesson, we will just focus on computing the determinant.

\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot 6-2\cdot 5 \\  & =18-10 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

The "square of a sum" formula states that

$$
x^2 + {\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{a}} x + a^2 =  (x+{\color{blue}{a}})^2 .
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
x^2 + 12x + 36.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+12x+{6}^{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula with ${\color{blue}{a}} = {\color{blue}{6}}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+6)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The "square of a difference" formula states that

$$
p^2 - {\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{a}} p + a^2 =  (p-{\color{blue}{a}})^2 .
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
p^2 - 10p + 25.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{2}-10p+{5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{2}-2\cdot 5p+{5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula with ${\color{blue}{a}} = {\color{blue}{5}}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
